designs.title: Probably Fine
designs.why: The strongest instant read of the three: a dense grid of 20 icons and a heavy deadpan line, legible from across the street on black. Line weight and condensed labels are consistent and print-safe. The weakness is that it looks like a clean vector icon pack. Nothing is drawn by a hand, so it reads more like a reference chart than a piece of graphic culture, and the 'all lit' idea never shows because the icons are plain outlines.
designs.fix: Give it a made-object finish: add short glow ticks around every icon so they read as lit, and rough up the line and type slightly, like a worn dash decal, so it feels drawn instead of downloaded.

designs.title: How to Go to Bed
designs.why: The best drawing here. The loose brush line has real character, the repeated 'Turn around.' is a quiet, well-timed joke, and the small sigh marks in step 7 pay it off. The serif italic captions suit the line. Problems: step 5 is a tangled pose that does not read as a dog at a glance, steps 6 and 7 are almost the same drawing, and on the tee the airy layout prints small and thin, so it gets lost on the chest.
designs.fix: Redraw step 5 as a clear mid-spin circle (head chasing tail) and tighten the spacing so the whole piece prints about 20% larger with more ink weight.

designs.title: The Box
designs.why: Crafted well: confident engraved-style line, a well-drawn tabby, and smart frame-breaking in panels 2 and 3. But the cat-picks-the-box gag is the most familiar joke of the three, and the narrow vertical strip of three boxed panels makes a skinny, small print with big empty margins on either side. Up close it reads as an instruction sheet, and from 3 m it is mostly boxes.
designs.fix: Make panel 3 the hero, large and frame-breaking, with panels 1 and 2 as small insets above it, so the payoff carries the shirt and the print fills the chest.
